title: Who Deleted Prod?
subtitle: 100 million customer records walked out the door, and every API call was made with our own role. Reconstruct the attack from CloudTrail, WAF logs and one very chatty metadata endpoint.

inspiredBy.title: Capital One data breach
inspiredBy.summary: In March 2019 an attacker abused a misconfigured web application firewall at Capital One to make server-side requests to the EC2 instance metadata service and obtained temporary credentials for the WAF's IAM role. With them she listed and copied S3 data on about 106 million credit card customers and applicants in the US and Canada. The breach was disclosed in July 2019, the bank was later fined 80 million US dollars, and AWS released IMDSv2 that November.

briefing:
**Thursday 19 November 2026, 14:30 UTC. Fernhill Credit, security team.**

This morning the statements portal started failing for every statement older than yesterday. Most of `fh-prod-customer-exports`, a week of full customer exports (about 100 million rows), is simply gone. Versioning was never on.

The incident channel already has suspects: an engineer who ran S3 deletes on Tuesday evening, a developer key that leaked on GitHub, maybe AWS itself. Security noticed something stranger: our own WAF instance role calling S3 with a user agent the WAF never uses.

The **evidence pack** holds the WAF log and config, CloudTrail, S3 server access logs, VPC flow logs, IAM and EC2 snapshots, GuardDuty, a change ticket and the Slack channel. **Read `README_FIRST.txt` first**, and mind the clocks: the WAF logs New York time, AWS logs UTC.

Six stages rebuild the attack: **the way in**, **when the keys were stolen**, **whose hands** held them, **what was taken**, **what deleted prod** and **why it was allowed**. Each answer is a small, exact value. Stuck? Use the Toolbox and the hints.
setupChecklist: Get the evidence: download and unzip the **evidence pack**, *or* open the **Evidence Explorer** to browse every file in your browser (no installs).
Read `README_FIRST.txt` end to end, including the glossary.
Note each source's clock: the WAF log is **US Eastern (-0500)**; CloudTrail, S3 access logs and GuardDuty are **UTC**; flow logs and Slack use **epoch seconds**.
Pick your path: **bash** with `jq` (Linux, macOS or WSL), **Windows PowerShell** (every Toolbox command has a PowerShell version), or the **browser Explorer**.
No AWS account needed. Everything in the pack is fictional, so don't try any of it against real systems.

evidence.description: Briefing from the incident lead, the file list, time-zone notes and a short AWS glossary. Start here.
Every request through the edge WAF / reverse proxy: client IP, request, status, bytes, user agent, the `upstream=` nginx connected to and the WAF verdict.
The WAF's `log_format`, its custom ModSecurity rules and its routes. Read it to understand each log field.
CloudTrail for 17 Nov, 22:00Z to midnight: one event per line, management and S3 data events.
CloudTrail for 18 Nov, midnight to 08:00Z. Most of the night happens here.
S3 server access log of the prod exports bucket, 18 Nov: remote IP, requester, operation, key, status, bytes.
The same bucket on 19 Nov, until 13:00Z.
Flow logs of the WAF instance's network interface, 10-minute aggregation. `start`/`end` are epoch seconds.
`aws ec2 describe-instances` for the WAF and the statements-api instances: addresses, instance profiles, metadata options.
The WAF instance role: trust policy, instance profile, attached and inline policies.
Long-lived IAM user access keys, their status and last use.
GuardDuty findings export. Active findings only.
GuardDuty suppression rules (filters that auto-archive findings).
The incident channel on 19 Nov. `ts` is epoch seconds as a string. Theories, not facts.
The change ticket for Tuesday evening's staging cleanup.

rules: Work only from the evidence pack. Don't read the generator source or the site's source code; that spoils the fun.
Answers are case-insensitive, and leading and trailing whitespace is ignored. Stick to the format shown under each question.

Hints cost the points shown on them and are revealed in order, from a gentle nudge to almost the full command. In the Toolbox, each command's syntax is free; seeing the full runnable command costs 5 points. Once you finish the case, every command is free.
Working in pairs is encouraged. Talk through your reasoning out loud, just like a real incident review.
Any tool is allowed: grep, awk, jq, Python, a spreadsheet, your favourite editor. The Toolbox tab lists commands that help.
Each wrong answer costs 2 points (at most 20 per stage), so check your reasoning before you submit. Try to be able to explain *why* your answer is right.

Speed and care pay: a fast solve earns a time bonus (up to +30 per stage, fading after the stage's target time), a clean solve with no hints, commands or wrong answers earns +10, the first player to solve a stage gets +15 first blood, and finishing all six stages without revealing an answer earns +50.
Don't share flags with other teams until everyone is done. Sharing techniques is fine.
Every IP, account id and key in the pack is fictional. Investigate the logs; don't point any of it at a real system.

stage.name: The way in
stage.goal: Find the client IP whose request through the WAF got a successful answer from the instance metadata service.
lookFor: `waf/access.log` has an `upstream=` field: where nginx really connected
The metadata service lives at 169.254.169.254, but an address can be written more than one way
Blocked requests (`waf=block`, 403) never reached it
Only a 200 counts as success
stage.explorerTip: Open `waf/access.log` and add a **contains** filter `upstream=169.254.169.254`, then a **regex** filter `" 200 `. Run **Count unique** with the regex `^(\S+)` to list the client IPs that remain. Now compare with a plain **contains** `169.254.169.254` filter: how is the address written in the requests that got through?

questions.title: The way in
questions.prompt:
Someone made our WAF talk to the EC2 instance metadata service (`169.254.169.254`), the internal endpoint that hands out the instance role's credentials. Plenty of scanners tried that night.

**Which client IP actually got a successful (HTTP 200) answer from it** through the WAF?

Answer with the IPv4 address.

hints.text: `grep 169.254.169.254` finds plenty of probes from several IPs, all blocked with 403. The requests that worked may not contain that string in the URL at all. Open `waf/edge-waf.conf`: which log field records where nginx *really* connected?

Filter on the `upstream=` field instead of the URL, keep only status `200` (field `$9`), then list the client IPs (field `$1`). Look at how those URLs spell the address: a single decimal number is a valid IPv4 address too.

questions.successNote:
Blocklists match strings, not destinations. Rule `100231` looked for the text `169.254.169.254`, while the attacker wrote the same address as one decimal number and walked straight past it. The real bug is `proxy_pass $arg_u`: a proxy that fetches any URL a stranger hands it. Fixes: an allowlist of destination hosts, checking the **resolved IP** after DNS, and blocking link-local ranges at the network layer.

Notice the warm-up too: harmless URLs first, then a request to the attacker's own server on port 8000. The flow logs show the WAF connecting **out** to it, the classic out-of-band SSRF test.

stage.name: When were the keys stolen?
stage.goal: Find the UTC time of the first request that returned the role's temporary credentials.
lookFor: `.../iam/security-credentials/` on its own only lists the role name
The keys come from `.../security-credentials/<role-name>`
The WAF logs US Eastern time (-0500)
Late evening in New York is already the next day in UTC
stage.explorerTip: In `waf/access.log`, filter **contains** `security-credentials/` and **contains** your stage 1 IP. Look at the response sizes, pick the right path, use **First match**, then turn the `-0500` time into UTC with the **time converter**.

questions.title: When were the keys stolen?
questions.prompt:
The metadata service hands out credentials at `/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name>`.

When did the attacker **first** successfully retrieve the role's credentials?

Answer with the time **in UTC** as `HH:MM:SS` (no date).

hints.text: Two paths look alike. The one ending in `security-credentials/` returns only the role name (look at its tiny response size). Only the one with the role name appended returns keys, and the attacker fetched it more than once.
Take the **earliest** such line with status 200 from your stage 1 IP. Its time is EST (`-0500`): add five hours, and expect the date to change.

```sh
grep -F 'upstream=169.254.169.254' waf/access.log \
  | awk '$9 == 200 && $7 ~ /security-credentials\/[^\/]+$/ {print $4, $5}'
date -u -d '17 Nov 2026 HH:MM:SS -0500' +%H:%M:%S
```

questions.successNote:
IMDSv1 answers any plain `GET` from inside the instance, including one your own reverse proxy makes for a stranger. **IMDSv2** demands a session token that must first be requested with a `PUT` carrying a special header, which a URL-fetching SSRF like this one cannot send. `ec2/describe-instances.json` shows `HttpTokens: optional` on the WAF and `required` on the newer instances.

CloudTrail even labels such sessions: `ec2RoleDelivery: 1.0` means the credentials were delivered by IMDSv1. That is worth an alert on its own.

stage.name: Whose hands?
stage.goal: Find the temporary access key id that was used by someone other than the WAF instance.
lookFor: For an EC2 instance role, the CloudTrail session name is the instance id
Role credentials rotate: the instance itself uses several keys during the night
`ec2/describe-instances.json` gives the instance's own addresses
Same role, same key, different `sourceIPAddress` and `userAgent`
stage.explorerTip: Open the 18 Nov CloudTrail file and add the **JSON field filter** `userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName = <role-name>`. Run **Count unique** with the regex `"sourceIPAddress":"([^"]+)"`, then add a **NOT** filter for the instance's own public IP and **Count unique** with `"accessKeyId":"(\w+)"`.

questions.title: Whose hands?
questions.prompt:
Every suspicious call in CloudTrail is signed by our own WAF instance role, and the instance uses that role all night long too.

**Which temporary access key id (`ASIA...`) was used by someone who was not the instance?**

Answer with the 20-character key id.
questions.answerFormat: Access key id (20 chars, starts with ASIA)

hints.text: Find the WAF instance's own public and private IP in `ec2/describe-instances.json` (match its instance profile to the role in `iam/roles/`). Anything the role does from any other address deserves a hard look.

Group the role's events by `sourceIPAddress`, `userAgent` and `userIdentity.accessKeyId`. You will see three keys, because IMDS rotates them. Only one of them also shows up from an address that isn't the instance, with a very different client.

questions.successNote:
Role credentials are bearer tokens: whoever holds them *is* the role, from anywhere on the internet. CloudTrail can't tell you *who* is behind a session, only **where** each call came from and **which client** made it. Here the very same key was used from the WAF's address by a Go log shipper and, at the same time, from an unknown address by `aws-cli`. That pattern is exactly what GuardDuty's `InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS` finding detects. Ours went straight to the archive: a 2024 suppression rule muted every finding for this role.

Note also that the API calls came from a **different IP** than the SSRF. A data-perimeter condition such as `aws:SourceVpce` (the statements-api role has one) would have made the stolen keys useless outside our network.

stage.name: What was taken?
stage.goal: Count the distinct objects the stolen credentials downloaded successfully.
lookFor: Only `GetObject` events without an `errorCode`
Count objects (bucket + key), not calls: some files were fetched twice
Filter on where the call came from, not only on the key: the instance used the same key
Every bucket counts, not just prod
stage.explorerTip: In the 18 Nov CloudTrail file, filter **contains** the address the stolen key was used from, **contains** `"eventName":"GetObject"`, and add a **NOT** filter `errorCode`. Then run **Count unique** with the regex `arn:aws:s3:::([^"/]+/[^"]+)` (the object ARN is bucket + key): the number of unique values is your answer.

questions.title: What was taken?
questions.prompt:
How much did they take?

Count the **distinct objects** (bucket + key) that the stolen credentials **successfully** downloaded with `GetObject`, across **all buckets**. Failed attempts don't count, and a file downloaded twice counts once.

Answer with an integer.

hints.text: Start from the events you isolated in stage 3: the role, used from outside. Keep only `GetObject` without an `errorCode`. `AccessDenied` and `NoSuchKey` are attempts, not downloads.

Build `bucket/key` from `requestParameters` and dedupe with `sort -u`. Don't filter on the access key alone: the instance read its own config files with that very key. You can cross-check the prod part with `s3-access-logs/` (`REST.GET.OBJECT`, status 200, the attacker's IP).

```sh
cat cloudtrail/*.jsonl | jq -r 'select(.sourceIPAddress == "<api-ip>" and .eventName == "GetObject" and (has("errorCode") | not))
  | "\(.requestParameters.bucketName)/\(.requestParameters.key)"' | sort -u | wc -l
```

questions.successNote:
This number drives the breach notification: which customers, which data, which regulators. Count **objects**, not requests, and only the ones that succeeded. The attacker also went for the cardholder vault and was stopped because the role had no `kms:Decrypt` on the vault's key. That is worth saying out loud in the report: a KMS key with its own policy is a real second wall. Plain SSE-S3 is not, because S3 decrypts for anyone allowed to `GetObject`.

The attacker also copied the WAF's own rules and config, which tells you they were studying the defences.

stage.name: Who deleted prod?
stage.goal: Find the API call that actually made prod's objects disappear.
lookFor: The S3 access log shows *how* the objects disappeared and who the requester was
`Delete*` calls on prod were attempted: did any of them succeed?
Some API calls change what S3 will do later, not right now
The staging cleanup happened on different buckets
stage.explorerTip: Open `s3-access-logs/fh-prod-customer-exports/2026-11-19.log` and run **Count unique** with the regex `\] \S+ \S+ \S+ (\S+)` to list the operations. Then open the 18 Nov CloudTrail file, filter **contains** the attacker's API address, add **contains** `"readOnly":false` and a **NOT** filter `errorCode`.

questions.title: Who deleted prod?
questions.prompt:
By 19 Nov most of the objects were gone, yet no `DeleteObject` or `DeleteBucket` on prod ever succeeded.

**Which API call actually destroyed prod's data?**

Answer with its `eventName`, **exactly as CloudTrail logs it**.

hints.text: Look at the operation column of the 19 Nov S3 access log. The deletions there have no IP address and the requester is `AmazonS3`: S3 removed the objects itself, because something told it to.

The attacker's `DeleteObject` and `DeleteBucket` calls failed with `AccessDenied` (an explicit deny). Look at what the same source did next, on the same bucket, that succeeded and was not read-only. Yoni's look-alike call on Tuesday was on a staging bucket.

questions.successNote:
A deny list is only as good as the actions it names. The role had an explicit deny on `s3:DeleteObject` and `s3:DeleteBucket` for `fh-prod-*`, so the attacker had S3 do the deleting: a bucket rule that expires every object after one day. S3 removed the objects on its own schedule, after midnight UTC. Those removals appear in the S3 server access log as `S3.EXPIRE.OBJECT` by `AmazonS3`, and **never** in CloudTrail as deletes. That is why grepping CloudTrail for `Delete` pointed at Yoni.

Protect buckets that matter with **versioning plus Object Lock** (or MFA delete), deny bucket-configuration changes as well as deletes, and alert on every one of them.

stage.name: Why was it allowed?
stage.goal: Find the policy statement that granted the call from stage 5.
lookFor: `iam/roles/fh-waf-edge-role.json` holds the role's inline policy
CloudTrail event names are not always IAM action names
A statement must match both the action and the resource
An explicit deny wins, but only for the actions it lists
stage.explorerTip: Open `iam/roles/fh-waf-edge-role.json` and read each statement's `Sid`, `Effect`, `Action` and `Resource`. Translate your stage 5 event into its IAM action (Toolbox: *API names vs IAM action names*), then test it against every `Action` pattern and check that the `Resource` covers the bucket ARN.

questions.title: Why was it allowed?
questions.prompt:
The WAF only ever needed to read its rules and ship its logs.

**Which statement in the role's inline policy allowed the call from stage 5?**

Answer with the statement's `Sid`, exactly as written.

hints.text: CloudTrail logs the API operation, but IAM authorizes an **action**, and for S3 bucket-configuration APIs the two names differ. Look your stage 5 event up in the AWS Service Authorization Reference for Amazon S3.

The action you need is `s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration`, on the resource `arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>`. Which `Allow` statement has an `Action` pattern that matches it *and* a `Resource` that covers the bucket? Does any `Deny` name it?

```sh
jq -r '.RolePolicies[].PolicyDocument.Statement[] | [.Sid, .Effect, (.Action | tostring), (.Resource | tostring)] | @tsv' \
  iam/roles/fh-waf-edge-role.json
[[ s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration == <pattern> ]] && echo matches   # try each Action pattern
```

questions.successNote:
Wildcards age badly. A *temporary* `s3:Put*` on `*`, added for a 2024 log migration and never removed, quietly included `s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration`, `s3:PutBucketPolicy` and every other `Put` on every bucket in the account. Next to `s3:Get*` and `s3:List*` on `*`, a WAF role became a read-and-reconfigure-everything role, and the delete-only deny never stood a chance.

The whole chain: **SSRF** in the WAF's preview proxy, **IMDSv1** answering it, an **over-broad role**, and **no detection** because the findings were suppressed. Break any one link and this story ends much earlier. Least privilege means named actions on named resources, plus data-perimeter conditions; IAM Access Analyzer's unused-access findings and policy generation make it practical.

items.title: Unpack the evidence
items.explain: Extracts the pack. Everything lives under one top-level folder.

items.title: See what you've got
items.explain: Every file with its size. The big ones (WAF log, flow logs, CloudTrail) are the ones you will filter, not read.

items.title: Read the README
items.explain: Time zones, formats and a glossary. Read it before anything else.

items.title: Peek at the first lines
items.explain: Look at a format **before** you parse it. `tail -n 3` shows the end of the window.

items.title: How big is it?
items.explain: Line counts tell you whether to eyeball a file or aggregate it.

items.title: Literal search
items.explain: `-F` treats the pattern as plain text, so the dots in an IP are dots, not "any character". It only finds the address **spelled exactly that way**.

items.title: Count matches
items.explain: `-c` prints how many lines match. Fast sanity checks.

items.title: Invert / exclude
items.explain: `-v` keeps lines that do **not** match. Each `-e` adds a pattern. Good for peeling off noise.

items.title: Print only the match
items.syntaxPowershell: Select-String -Path <log-file> -Pattern '<field>=<regex>' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.explain: `-o` outputs just the matched text. Here: every upstream nginx connected to, with counts. Rare values deserve a look.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path waf\access.log -Pattern 'upstream=\S+' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Search several files at once
items.explain: `-h` drops the file name prefix so the output is still valid JSON lines you can pipe into `jq`.

items.title: Context around a hit
items.explain: `-B`/`-A` show lines before and after each match: what else happened around that moment?

items.title: Pull fields from WAF lines
items.explain: Split on spaces: `$1` client IP, `$4 $5` time and offset, `$7` URI, `$9` status, `$10` bytes. The user agent contains spaces, so for later fields use `grep -o 'upstream=[^ ]*'` instead of counting.

items.title: Status code histogram
items.syntaxPowershell: Select-String -Path <waf-log> -Pattern '<status-regex-with-group>' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.explain: How many of each status. The classic first look at any access log.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path waf\access.log -Pattern '" (\d{3}) ' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Top client IPs
items.syntaxPowershell: Select-String -Path <waf-log> -Pattern '<ip-regex-with-group>' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First <count> Count, Name
items.command: awk '{print $1}' waf/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
items.explain: Who talks to us the most? Attackers are often *not* at the top: they make few, precise requests.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path waf\access.log -Pattern '^(\S+)' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First 20 Count, Name

items.title: Filter by field, then by text
items.explain: awk compares a field exactly (`200` won't match inside a byte count), then grep narrows by path.

items.title: What did the WAF block?
items.syntaxPowershell: Select-String -Path <waf-log> -Pattern '<block-marker> <field>=(<regex>)' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Select-Object Count, Name
items.explain: Which custom rules fired, and how often. Then read those rules in `waf/edge-waf.conf`: what exactly do they match?
items.powershell: Select-String -Path waf\access.log -Pattern 'waf=block rule=(\d+)' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: First and last occurrence
items.explain: Start and end of a phenomenon in one go. The log is in time order.

items.title: Pretty-print one event
items.explain: See every field a CloudTrail record carries: `userIdentity`, `sourceIPAddress`, `userAgent`, `eventName`, `requestParameters`, `errorCode`...

items.title: Which API calls happened?
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <cloudtrail-files> | ConvertFrom-Json | Group-Object <field> | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.command: cat cloudtrail/*.jsonl | jq -r '.eventName' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
items.explain: A histogram of `eventName`. Rare write calls stand out.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Group-Object eventName | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Who signed the calls?
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <cloudtrail-files> | ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { if ($_.<path>) { $_.<path> } else { $_.<fallback-path> } } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.command: cat cloudtrail/*.jsonl | jq -r '.userIdentity.arn // .userIdentity.type' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
items.explain: Principals by volume. For an assumed role the ARN ends in the session name; for an EC2 instance role that is the instance id.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { if ($_.userIdentity.arn) { $_.userIdentity.arn } else { $_.userIdentity.type } } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Who, from where, with which key
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <cloudtrail-files> | ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { '{0} {1} {2}' -f $_.<path>, $_.<path>, $_.<path> } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.command: cat cloudtrail/*.jsonl | jq -r '[.userIdentity.arn // "-", .sourceIPAddress, .userIdentity.accessKeyId // "-"] | @tsv' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
items.explain: Groups events by principal, source IP and access key. One principal should normally come from a small, predictable set of places.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { '{0} {1} {2}' -f $_.userIdentity.arn, $_.sourceIPAddress, $_.userIdentity.accessKeyId } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Which client made the call?
items.syntax: cat <cloudtrail-files> | jq -r '[.<field>, .<field>[0:<length>]] | @tsv' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -<count>
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <cloudtrail-files> | ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { '{0} {1}' -f $_.<field>, $_.<field>.Substring(0, [Math]::Min(<length>, $_.<field>.Length)) } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First <count> Count, Name
items.command: cat cloudtrail/*.jsonl | jq -r '[.sourceIPAddress, .userAgent[0:40]] | @tsv' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
items.explain: The `userAgent` tells you the SDK or tool. A service written in Go doesn't suddenly start using a Python CLI.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { '{0} {1}' -f $_.sourceIPAddress, $_.userAgent.Substring(0, [Math]::Min(40, $_.userAgent.Length)) } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First 20 Count, Name

items.title: Only one role
items.explain: `sessionIssuer.userName` is the role behind an assumed-role session, whatever the session is called.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Where-Object { $_.userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName -eq '<role-name>' } | Select-Object -First 10 eventTime, eventName, sourceIPAddress

items.title: Exclude known sources
items.explain: Drop the addresses you can explain and see what's left.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Where-Object { $_.sourceIPAddress -notin @('<ip>', '<other-ip>') } | Select-Object -First 10 eventTime, eventName, sourceIPAddress

items.title: Failed calls
items.explain: `errorCode` exists only when a call failed. A failure is an attempt, not an action, but attempts show intent.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Where-Object { $_.errorCode } | Format-Table eventTime, eventName, errorCode, sourceIPAddress

items.title: One actor's timeline
items.explain: Everything one source did, in order, with the target bucket and whether it worked. `readOnly` is false for calls that change something.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Where-Object { $_.sourceIPAddress -eq '<ip>' } | Format-Table eventTime, eventName, @{n='bucket'; e={$_.requestParameters.bucketName}}, errorCode, readOnly

items.title: Distinct objects read
items.syntax: cat <cloudtrail-files> | jq -r 'select(.<field> == "<value>" and (has("<field>") | not)) | "\(.<path>)/\(.<path>)"' | sort -u | wc -l
items.command: cat cloudtrail/*.jsonl | jq -r 'select(.eventName == "GetObject" and (has("errorCode") | not)) | "\(.requestParameters.bucketName)/\(.requestParameters.key)"' | sort -u | wc -l
items.explain: Builds `bucket/key` for every successful `GetObject` and counts unique ones. Add your own `select()` conditions for *who*.
items.powershell: (Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Where-Object { $_.eventName -eq 'GetObject' -and -not $_.errorCode } | ForEach-Object { $_.requestParameters.bucketName + '/' + $_.requestParameters.key } | Sort-Object -Unique | Measure-Object).Count

items.title: S3 access log fields
items.explain: `$2` bucket, `$3 $4` time (UTC), `$5` remote IP, `$6` requester (ARN, or a service), `$7` request id, `$8` operation, `$9` key. Status follows the quoted request line.

items.title: Operations histogram
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <s3-access-logs> | ForEach-Object { ($_ -split ' ')[<operation-index>] } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.explain: `REST.GET.OBJECT`, `REST.PUT.OBJECT`, ... and operations S3 performs on its own. Which ones only appear on one day?
items.powershell: Get-Content s3-access-logs\*\*.log | ForEach-Object { ($_ -split ' ')[7] } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Who touched the bucket, from where
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <s3-access-logs> | ForEach-Object { $f = $_ -split ' '; "$($f[<index>]) $($f[<index>])" } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.explain: Remote IP and requester together. The same requester ARN from two very different networks is a red flag.
items.powershell: Get-Content s3-access-logs\*\*.log | ForEach-Object { $f = $_ -split ' '; "$($f[4]) $($f[5])" } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: One source's requests
items.explain: Every request from one IP: time, operation and key.

items.title: Bytes sent
items.command: awk '$5 == "<ip>" && $8 == "REST.GET.OBJECT"' s3-access-logs/*/*.log | grep -oE 'HTTP/1.1" 200 - [0-9]+' | awk '{s += $NF} END {print s}'
items.explain: Sums the bytes S3 sent for successful object reads. Useful for the breach report.
items.powershell: Get-Content s3-access-logs\*\*.log | Where-Object { ($_ -split ' ')[4] -eq '<ip>' } | Select-String 'REST.GET.OBJECT .*HTTP/1.1" 200 - (\d+)' | ForEach-Object { [long]$_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Measure-Object -Sum

items.title: Number the columns
items.explain: Flow log v2: `$4` srcaddr, `$5` dstaddr, `$6` srcport, `$7` dstport, `$10` bytes, `$11`/`$12` start/end (epoch), `$13` action.

items.title: All flows with one host
items.explain: Both directions. Convert `start` with `date -u -d @<epoch>`.

items.title: Connections the instance started
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <flow-log> | Select-Object -Skip 1 | ForEach-Object { $f = $_ -split ' '; if ($f[<src-index>] -like '<network-prefix>*' -and $f[<port-index>] -ne '<port>') { $f[<index>] + ':' + $f[<index>] } } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
items.explain: A WAF mostly *answers* on 443. Flows where it is the source and the source port is not 443 are connections it opened itself. Where to?
items.powershell: Get-Content vpc-flow-logs\*.log | Select-Object -Skip 1 | ForEach-Object { $f = $_ -split ' '; if ($f[3] -like '10.*' -and $f[5] -ne '443') { $f[4] + ':' + $f[6] } } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Rejected probes
items.syntaxPowershell: Get-Content <flow-log> | Where-Object { ($_ -split ' ')[<action-index>] -eq '<action>' } | ForEach-Object { $f = $_ -split ' '; "$($f[<index>]) $($f[<index>])" } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First <count> Count, Name
items.command: awk '$13 == "REJECT" {print $4, $7}' vpc-flow-logs/*.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
items.explain: What the security group dropped. Port scans are loud, common and usually not the story.
items.powershell: Get-Content vpc-flow-logs\*.log | Where-Object { ($_ -split ' ')[12] -eq 'REJECT' } | ForEach-Object { $f = $_ -split ' '; "$($f[3]) $($f[6])" } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 Count, Name

items.title: nginx time to UTC
items.explain: Turns `[dd/Mon/yyyy:HH:MM:SS -0500]` into an ISO UTC time. Watch the date: it may roll over.

items.title: EST to UTC
items.explain: In November, New York is UTC-05:00. Add five hours.

items.title: UTC to EST
items.explain: What a UTC instant was on the New York office clock.

items.title: Epoch to UTC
items.explain: For flow logs and Slack. On macOS: `date -u -r 1794952800`.

items.title: Read the Slack channel
items.explain: Slack `ts` is an epoch string. `tonumber | floor | todate` gives ISO-8601 UTC.

items.title: Decimal number to IPv4
items.explain: An IPv4 address is just a 32-bit number. `http://3232235777/` and `http://192.168.1.1/` go to the same place, and string blocklists rarely know that.

items.title: URL-decode a parameter
items.explain: `%3A` is `:`, `%2F` is `/`. Decode before you decide what a request was really asking for.

items.title: Instances, addresses, IMDS settings
items.command: jq '.Reservations[].Instances[] | {InstanceId, PrivateIpAddress, PublicIpAddress, profile: .IamInstanceProfile.Arn, MetadataOptions}' ec2/describe-instances.json
items.explain: Which instance profile each instance wears, its own IPs, and whether IMDSv2 is enforced (`HttpTokens: required`).
items.powershell: (Get-Content ec2\describe-instances.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json).Reservations.Instances | Select-Object InstanceId, PrivateIpAddress, PublicIpAddress, @{n='profile'; e={$_.IamInstanceProfile.Arn}}, @{n='HttpTokens'; e={$_.MetadataOptions.HttpTokens}}

items.title: Policy statements at a glance
items.explain: One line per statement: Sid, Effect, Action and Resource. Wildcards (`*`) are where the surprises live.
items.powershell: (Get-Content iam\roles\<role-name>.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json).RolePolicies.PolicyDocument.Statement | Format-Table Sid, Effect, @{n='Action'; e={$_.Action -join ','}}, @{n='Resource'; e={$_.Resource -join ','}} -Wrap

items.title: API names vs IAM action names
items.explain: CloudTrail logs the **API operation**; IAM authorizes an **action**, and for S3 they don't always match. `ListObjects` (V2) needs `s3:ListBucket`; `ListBuckets` needs `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`; several bucket-configuration APIs have their own action names. Check each one in the AWS Service Authorization Reference for Amazon S3.
items.powershell: Get-Content cloudtrail\*.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Where-Object { $_.eventSource -eq 's3.amazonaws.com' } | Select-Object -ExpandProperty eventName -Unique

items.title: Does a wildcard cover an action?
items.explain: IAM `Action` and `Resource` patterns are globs: `*` matches any run of characters. Test the action and the resource ARN against every statement, and remember that an explicit `Deny` beats any `Allow`.

items.title: Long-lived keys
items.explain: IAM user keys (`AKIA...`) and their status. Temporary role credentials (`ASIA...`) never appear here.

debrief: _Sealed._ Finish all six stages to unlock the debrief.
